claim: Parkinson's disease (PD) affects 1–2% of the population over 60 years old, and 4% above 85 years of age.
source: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disorder, affecting 1–2% of the population over 60 years old, and 4% above 85 years of age (Coppedè, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Coppedè, 2012, which provides epidemiological data on PD prevalence.

claim: The main symptoms of PD are muscle rigidity, bradykinesia, resting tremor, and postural instability and may be accompanied by sleep disorders, anosmia, depression, and dementia.
source: The main symptoms of PD are muscle rigidity, bradykinesia, resting tremor, and postural instability and may be accompanied by sleep disorders, anosmia, depression, and dementia (Sironi et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sironi et al., 2020, which describes the clinical symptoms of PD.

claim: PD is characterised by a progressive and selective degeneration of dopaminergic (DA) neurons of the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNpc).
source: It is characterised by a progressive and selective degeneration of dopaminergic (DA) neurons of the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNpc).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the pathological hallmark of Parkinson's disease.

claim: There are currently no treatments available that modify the course of neurodegenerative decline in PD.
source: Currently, there are no treatments available that modify the course of neurodegenerative decline.
evidence: This reflects the current state of clinical knowledge about PD treatment limitations.

claim: About 15% of PD cases appear to be inherited.
source: Although this disease is mostly sporadic, about 15% of cases appear to be inherited and in support of this, 20 genes implicated in PD have been identified from familial genetic studies while ~90 loci have been identified from PD-GWAS (Deng et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Deng et al., 2018, which provides genetic epidemiology data.

claim: 20 genes implicated in PD have been identified from familial genetic studies.
source: Although this disease is mostly sporadic, about 15% of cases appear to be inherited and in support of this, 20 genes implicated in PD have been identified from familial genetic studies while ~90 loci have been identified from PD-GWAS (Deng et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Deng et al., 2018, which summarizes genetic findings in PD.

claim: Approximately 90 loci have been identified from PD-GWAS.
source: Although this disease is mostly sporadic, about 15% of cases appear to be inherited and in support of this, 20 genes implicated in PD have been identified from familial genetic studies while ~90 loci have been identified from PD-GWAS (Deng et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Deng et al., 2018, which reports GWAS findings.

claim: Evidence strongly links impaired mitochondrial and lysosomal function to PD pathology.
source: The exact causes of PD are currently unknown but some evidence strongly links impaired mitochondrial and lysosomal function to disease pathology (Sironi et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sironi et al., 2020, which reviews evidence linking organellar dysfunction to PD.

claim: Mutations in PARK8, encoding for LRRK2, are the most frequently reported cause of PD.
source: Mutations in PARK8, encoding for LRRK2 (Leucine-Rich Repeat Kinase 2), are the most frequently reported cause of PD (Bouhouche et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bouhouche et al., 2017, which reports on the frequency of LRRK2 mutations in PD.

claim: The LRRK2 G2019S mutation represents 4% of familial and 1% of sporadic PD cases.
source: The most common mutation associated with PD is the substitution of glycine at position 2019 of LRRK2 to serine (G2019S), representing 4% of familial and 1% of sporadic cases (Lill, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lill, 2016, which provides epidemiological data on G2019S prevalence.

claim: LRRK2 is a large multidomain protein with two catalytic domains: a ROC GTPase domain and a kinase domain.
source: LRRK2 is a large multidomain protein with two catalytic domains: a Ras of complex (ROC) GTPase domain that is able to bind GTP and hydrolyse it, and a kinase domain that utilises a subset of Rab GTPases as substrates (Steger et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Steger et al., 2016, which characterizes LRRK2 structure and function.

claim: The LRRK2 kinase domain utilises a subset of Rab GTPases as substrates.
source: LRRK2 is a large multidomain protein with two catalytic domains: a Ras of complex (ROC) GTPase domain that is able to bind GTP and hydrolyse it, and a kinase domain that utilises a subset of Rab GTPases as substrates (Steger et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Steger et al., 2016, which identified Rab GTPases as LRRK2 substrates.

claim: All segregating mutations associated with PD are located in the catalytic core of LRRK2.
source: Importantly, all the segregating mutations associated with PD are located in the catalytic core.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the location of pathogenic LRRK2 mutations.

claim: Mutations in the ROC/COR domain (R1441C/G/H or Y1699C) lead to decreased GTPase activity and elevated kinase activity.
source: A mutation in the ROC/COR domain, such as the R1441C/G/H or the Y1699C mutation, leads to decreased GTPase activity and elevated kinase activity (Rudenko and Cookson, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rudenko and Cookson, 2014, which characterizes the biochemical effects of these mutations.

claim: Mutations in the kinase domain (G2019S or I2020T) lead to elevated kinase activity.
source: Mutations in the kinase domain, such as the G2019S or the I2020T, also lead to an elevated kinase activity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the biochemical consequences of kinase domain mutations.

claim: Enhanced kinase activity appears to be a common factor in pathogenic LRRK2 mutations.
source: Hence, enhanced kinase activity appears to be a common factor in pathogenic LRRK2 mutations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that multiple different pathogenic mutations all result in increased kinase activity.

claim: Mounting evidence implicates LRRK2 in membrane trafficking.
source: Although the function of LRRK2 within cells is currently unknown, mounting evidence implicates a role in membrane trafficking (Steger et al., 2016; Pfeffer, 2018; Hur et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Steger et al., 2016; Pfeffer, 2018; Hur et al., 2019, which provide evidence for LRRK2's role in membrane trafficking.

claim: Macroautophagy is a membrane trafficking pathway that delivers intracellular components to the lysosome for degradation.
source: Macroautophagy is a membrane trafficking pathway that delivers intracellular components to the lysosome for degradation (Yu et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yu et al., 2018, which describes the autophagy pathway.

claim: Mitophagy is the autophagic turnover of mitochondria.
source: The autophagic turnover of mitochondria is termed mitophagy, which acts as a mitochondrial quality control mechanism that allows the selective degradation of damaged or unnecessary mitochondria (Rodger et al., 2018; Montava-Garriga and Ganley, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rodger et al., 2018; Montava-Garriga and Ganley, 2020, which define and describe mitophagy.

claim: Mitophagy acts as a mitochondrial quality control mechanism that allows the selective degradation of damaged or unnecessary mitochondria.
source: The autophagic turnover of mitochondria is termed mitophagy, which acts as a mitochondrial quality control mechanism that allows the selective degradation of damaged or unnecessary mitochondria (Rodger et al., 2018; Montava-Garriga and Ganley, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rodger et al., 2018; Montava-Garriga and Ganley, 2020, which describe the function of mitophagy.

claim: PINK1 and Parkin sequentially operate to initiate mitophagy in response to mitochondrial depolarisation in cell lines.
source: Mitophagy itself has strong links to PD following the landmark discoveries that PINK1 and Parkin, two other genes mutated in familial PD, sequentially operate to initiate mitophagy in response to mitochondrial depolarisation in cell lines (Narendra et al., 2008; Koyano et al., 2014; Pickrell and Youle, 2015; Yamano et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Narendra et al., 2008; Koyano et al., 2014; Pickrell and Youle, 2015; Yamano et al., 2018, which describe the PINK1/Parkin pathway.

claim: PINK1 and Parkin are not required for regulation of mitophagy under normal, or basal, conditions.
source: However, when this pathway becomes relevant in vivo, and under what physiological conditions, is unclear especially given that PINK1 and Parkin are not required for regulation of mitophagy under normal, or basal, conditions (McWilliams et al., 2018a; McWilliams et al., 2018b; Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to McWilliams et al., 2018a; McWilliams et al., 2018b; Lee et al., 2018, which demonstrate that PINK1/Parkin are not required for basal mitophagy.

claim: LRRK2 G2019S mutation is associated with reduced mitophagy in primary MEFs.
source: However, we observed that LRRK2 G2019S KI mutant cells displayed significantly lower basal mitophagy levels, whereas the absence of LRRK2 (KO) led to an increase of this process.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and C, demonstrating reduced mitophagy in G2019S MEFs.

claim: LRRK2 knockout leads to increased basal mitophagy in primary MEFs.
source: However, we observed that LRRK2 G2019S KI mutant cells displayed significantly lower basal mitophagy levels, whereas the absence of LRRK2 (KO) led to an increase of this process.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and C, demonstrating increased mitophagy in LRRK2 KO MEFs.

claim: LRRK2 predominantly influences basal mitophagy as deferiprone and EBSS increased mitophagy to a similar level across all genotypes.
source: Interestingly, our data suggests that LRRK2 predominantly influences basal mitophagy as deferiprone (DFP) and long-term amino acid starvation in Earls Balanced Salt Solution (EBSS), both strong mitophagy inducers (Allen et al., 2013), increased mitophagy to a similar level across all genotypes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B, demonstrating similar mitophagy induction across genotypes with DFP and EBSS.

claim: The Lrrk2 genotype does not significantly alter basal autophagy in primary MEFs.
source: In contrast to mitophagy, in isolated primary MEFs we noticed no significant difference in the number of mCherry-only autolysosomes across all the Lrrk2 genotypes under basal conditions (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and F, demonstrating no significant difference in autophagy across genotypes.

claim: The Lrrk2 genotype does not significantly alter amino acid starvation-induced autophagy in primary MEFs.
source: A robust autophagy response was observed in all cells and as with basal autophagy, the Lrrk2 genotype failed to significantly alter this large increase in autolysosomes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, demonstrating similar autophagy induction across genotypes with EBSS.

claim: GSK3357679A stimulates mitophagy in a dose-dependent manner in WT primary MEFs with maximal stimulation at 10 nM.
source: We tested GSK3357679A in primary mito-QC MEFs and observed a dose-dependent effect on mitophagy with a maximal stimulation achieved at a concentration of 10 nM in WT cells (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G and H, demonstrating dose-dependent mitophagy stimulation.

claim: GSK3357679A-induced mitophagy stimulation is equivalent to the level of mitophagy observed in LRRK2 KO cells.
source: The level of stimulation was equivalent to the level of mitophagy observed in LRRK2 KO cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G and H, comparing GSK3357679A-treated WT cells to KO cells.

claim: GSK3357679A fails to alter mitophagy in the absence of LRRK2.
source: Importantly, GSK3357679A failed to alter mitophagy in the absence of LRRK2, demonstrating that its mitophagy-enhancing properties are dependent on LRRK2.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G and H, demonstrating no effect of GSK3357679A in LRRK2 KO cells.

claim: In G2019S cells, maximal effect of GSK3357679A on mitophagy is reached at 100 nM.
source: In the G2019S cells, we observed a reduced response, with a maximal effect on mitophagy reached at 100 nM and this may reflect the increased kinase activity of this mutant (Nichols et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G and H, demonstrating dose-response in G2019S cells.

claim: GSK3357679A potently inhibits LRRK2 kinase activity in a dose-dependent manner, as indicated by decreased phosphorylation of Rab10 at threonine 73.
source: Western blotting analysis confirmed that GSK3357679A potently inhibited LRRK2 kinase activity in a dose-dependent manner, as indicated by decreased phosphorylation of its substrate Rab10 at threonine 73 (Steger et al., 2016), as well as reduced LRRK2 S935 phosphorylation (an indirect measure of LRRK2 activity (Ito et al., 2016), Figure 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H, demonstrating dose-dependent reduction in Rab10 phosphorylation.

claim: GSK3357679A reduces LRRK2 S935 phosphorylation, an indirect measure of LRRK2 activity.
source: Western blotting analysis confirmed that GSK3357679A potently inhibited LRRK2 kinase activity in a dose-dependent manner, as indicated by decreased phosphorylation of its substrate Rab10 at threonine 73 (Steger et al., 2016), as well as reduced LRRK2 S935 phosphorylation (an indirect measure of LRRK2 activity (Ito et al., 2016), Figure 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H and a citation to Ito et al., 2016, which establishes S935 phosphorylation as a marker of LRRK2 activity.

claim: GSK2578215A and MLi-2 can inhibit LRRK2 in cells and increase mitophagy.
source: As with GSK3357679A, both these compounds were able to inhibit LRRK2 in cells and increase mitophagy (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E, demonstrating mitophagy induction by these inhibitors.

claim: At high concentrations, MLi2 fails to stimulate mitophagy, possibly due to off-target effects.
source: We do note that at high concentrations, MLi2 failed to stimulate mitophagy and this may be due to off-target effects, as at 20 nM it also inhibited mitophagy in the LRRK2 KO cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, demonstrating inhibition of mitophagy in KO cells at high MLi2 concentrations.

claim: GSK3357679A significantly increases co-localisation of mCherry-GFP-LC3 with ATPB at both the autophagosome and autolysosome stages.
source: Treatment of cells with GSK3357679A significantly increased co-localisation of mCherry-GFP-LC3 with ATPB, both at the autophagosome stage (GFP and mCherry-positive, Figure 2B) and autolysosome stage (mCherry-only positive, Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A, B, and C, demonstrating increased co-localisation.

claim: LRRK2 inhibition uses a canonical autophagy pathway to drive mitophagy.
source: This implies LRRK2 inhibition uses a canonical autophagy pathway to drive mitophagy.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that LC3 co-localizes with mitochondria upon LRRK2 inhibition.

claim: Mitophagy induction by GSK3357679A is blocked in ATG5 KO MEFs.
source: In the matched WT MEFs, GSK3357679A was able to induce mitophagy in a similar manner to the primary mito-QC MEFs; however, mitophagy induction was blocked in the ATG5 KO MEFs (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D, demonstrating no mitophagy induction in ATG5 KO cells.

claim: GSK3357679A treatment results in a significant 1.3-fold increase in autolysosomes containing mitochondria as observed by TEM.
source: Partially degraded mitochondrial structures could clearly be identified within autolysosomes (representative images shown in Figure 2E) and when quantified, a significant 1.3-fold increase was detected in the GSK3357679A-treated samples.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E and F, demonstrating increased mitolysosomes by TEM.

claim: LRRK2 inhibition stimulates mitophagy through canonical ATG5-dependent autophagy.
source: Taken together, the data show that LRRK2 inhibition stimulates mitophagy through canonical ATG5-dependent autophagy and confirms that the mito-QC reporter is measuring a conventional mitophagy pathway in this instance.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined data from LC3 co-localization, ATG5 dependency, and TEM observations.

claim: Treatment of PINK1 KO mito-QC MEFs with GSK3357679A results in a comparable increase in mitophagy to WT cells.
source: Treatment of litter-matched WT and PINK1 KO mito-QC MEFs with GSK3357679A resulted in a comparable increase in mitophagy regardless of the presence or absence of PINK1 (Figure 2G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G and H, demonstrating similar mitophagy induction in WT and PINK1 KO cells.

claim: No detectible increase in phospho-ubiquitin levels is observed following LRRK2 inhibition.
source: We observed no detectible increase in phospho-ubiquitin levels following LRRK2 inhibition, which contrasted with that observed following mitochondrial depolarisation with CCCP treatment (Figure 2I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I, demonstrating no change in phospho-ubiquitin with GSK3357679A.

claim: GSK3357679A treatment does not affect PINK1/Parkin-dependent mitophagy induced by CCCP.
source: mito-QC clearly detected a large and significant increase in mitophagy following mitochondrial depolarisation, but this was unaffected by GSK3357679A, as were phospho-ubiquitin levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–F, demonstrating no effect of GSK3357679A on CCCP-induced mitophagy.

claim: GSK3357679A treatment has no direct effect on the mitochondrial respiratory chain.
source: Thus, we activated the NADH- and succinate-linked pathway and injected sequentially incremental doses of GSK3357679A. This had no direct effect on the mitochondrial respiratory chain (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1H, demonstrating no change in respiration with acute GSK3357679A exposure.

claim: Chronic (24 hr) treatment with GSK3357679A does not affect mitochondrial respiration.
source: Secondly, we evaluated the chronic effects of LRRK2 inhibition by incubating immortalised MEFs for 24 hr with 10 nM GSK3357679A (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I). Despite an increase in mitophagy (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), we did not observe any difference in mitochondrial respiration.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1I, demonstrating no change in respiration with chronic GSK3357679A exposure.

claim: LRRK2 inhibition does not globally impact mitochondrial form or function at 24 hours.
source: Thus, LRRK2 inhibition does not globally impact mitochondrial form or function at this timepoint.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined TEM and respirometry data showing no changes in mitochondrial morphology or function.

claim: Basal mitophagy is significantly enhanced in LRRK2 KO dopaminergic neurons compared to WT.
source: Basal mitophagy was significantly enhanced in the LRRK2 KO neurons compared to WT, and although not statistically significant, mitophagy appeared reduced in DA neurons of LRRK2 G2019S KI mice compared to WT (Figure 3A and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and C, demonstrating increased mitophagy in LRRK2 KO DA neurons.

claim: Mitophagy is significantly reduced in G2019S dopaminergic neurons.
source: While we cannot say that mitophagy is significantly impaired in the G2019S DA neurons from this set of experiments using nine individual mice, we did however find a significant mitophagy reduction in G2019S DA neurons in a later set of experiments, with 10 mice per condition (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and B, demonstrating reduced mitophagy in G2019S DA neurons.

claim: No statistical difference in mitophagy in Purkinje cells is found between LRRK2 genotypes.
source: Contrary to what we observed in SNpc DA neurons, no statistical difference in mitophagy in Purkinje cells was found between any group (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and E, demonstrating no difference in mitophagy in Purkinje neurons.

claim: An enhanced presence of microglial cells is observed in the cortex of G2019S animals compared to WT or KO mice.
source: Notably, we observed an enhanced presence of microglial cells in the cortex of G2019S animals when compared to WT or KO mice (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and G, demonstrating increased microglial cell numbers in G2019S cortex.

claim: Basal mitophagy is significantly decreased in G2019S microglia compared to WT.
source: Regardless, when mitophagy quantitation was normalised for cell number (mitolysosomes per Iba1-positive cell body per field), we found a significant decrease in basal mitophagy in G2019S microglia compared to WT, as well as an increase in mitophagy levels in KO cells (Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and H, demonstrating reduced mitophagy in G2019S microglia.

claim: Mitophagy levels are increased in LRRK2 KO microglia compared to WT.
source: Regardless, when mitophagy quantitation was normalised for cell number (mitolysosomes per Iba1-positive cell body per field), we found a significant decrease in basal mitophagy in G2019S microglia compared to WT, as well as an increase in mitophagy levels in KO cells (Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and H, demonstrating increased mitophagy in LRRK2 KO microglia.

claim: Cortical astrocytes do not show any observable difference in mitophagy across Lrrk2 genotypes.
source: In contrast, cortical astrocytes, stained with glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP, Figure 3I), did not show any observable difference in mitophagy across Lrrk2 genotypes (Figure 3J).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I and J, demonstrating no difference in mitophagy in astrocytes.

claim: Analysis of auto-QC mouse brains indicates no change in general macroautophagy in DA neurons and microglia across Lrrk2 genotypes.
source: In contrast to the Lrrk2 genotype effects on mitophagy in DA neurons and microglia, analysis of auto-QC mouse brains indicated no change in general macroautophagy in these cell types (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1, demonstrating no change in autophagy in brain cells.

claim: Mitophagy is reduced in G2019S lungs and enhanced (over 2-fold relative to WT) in KO lungs.
source: Basal mitophagy across the whole lung was evident in all genotypes and in a similar fashion to MEFs, DA neurons and microglia, mitophagy was reduced in G2019S mice and enhanced (over 2-fold relative to WT) in KO mice (Figure 4A and B)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and B, demonstrating altered mitophagy in lungs across genotypes.

claim: Enlarged type II pneumocytes with considerable vesicular-like structures are observed in all LRRK2 KO animals.
source: As previously reported (Baptista et al., 2018; Plowey et al., 2008), we observed enlarged type II pneumocytes with considerable vesicular-like structures in all the animals of the LRRK2 KO group that is attributable to the accumulation of large lamellar bodies, which are secretory lysosomes responsible for surfactant release.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and citations to Baptista et al., 2018; Plowey et al., 2008, which previously reported this phenotype.

claim: There is a small decrease in mitophagy in G2019S-expressing kidney cortex tissue.
source: LRRK2-dependent mitophagy changes in the kidney were much lower in magnitude compared to the lung, yet there was a small decrease in G2019S-expressing tissue (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and D, demonstrating a small decrease in kidney mitophagy in G2019S mice.

claim: No significant difference in the number of autolysosomes is observed in the lungs of auto-QC reporter mice across Lrrk2 genotypes.
source: Consistent with brain and MEF data, no significant difference in the number of autolysosomes was observed in the lungs of auto-QC reporter mice (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and F, demonstrating no change in lung autophagy.

claim: No effect of Lrrk2 genotype on autolysosomes is detected in the kidney cortex.
source: Likewise, in the kidney cortex, we did not detect an effect of Lrrk2 genotype on autolysosomes (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G and H, demonstrating no change in kidney autophagy.

claim: The Lrrk2 genotype does not majorly affect all autophagy pathways but predominantly impacts basal mitophagy, both in vitro and in vivo.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that the Lrrk2 genotype does not majorly affect all autophagy pathways but predominantly impacts basal mitophagy, both in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined data showing specific effects on mitophagy but not general autophagy.

claim: GSK3357679A decreases the phosphorylation of LRRK2 on S935 and the phosphorylation of Rab12 on S106 in both WT and G2019S brains.
source: GSK3357679A decreased the phosphorylation of LRRK2 on S935 and the phosphorylation of Rab12 on S106, in both WT and G2019S mice (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and B, demonstrating reduced phosphorylation of LRRK2 and Rab12 in brain lysates.

claim: The level of Rab12 phosphorylation is higher in G2019S brains.
source: Interestingly, the level of Rab12 phosphorylation was higher in G2019S brains, which could reflect the higher kinase activity that is associated with this mutation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and B, demonstrating increased Rab12 phosphorylation in G2019S brains.

claim: PGC-1α is increased in the brains of G2019S mice.
source: Of potential relevance, we found that the mitochondrial biogenesis marker PGC-1α was increased in the brains of G2019S mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and C, demonstrating increased PGC-1α in G2019S brains.

claim: In both WT and G2019S brains, LRRK2 inhibition causes an increase in PGC-1β.
source: Additionally, in both WT and G2019S brains, LRRK2 inhibition caused a further increase in PGC-1β, suggesting a potential activation of mitochondrial biogenesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and C, demonstrating increased PGC-1β with GSK3357679A treatment.

claim: An increase of TFAm is observed following LRRK2 inhibition.
source: In confirmation, we observed an increase of the master regulator of mitochondrial biogenesis, TFAm (Ljubicic et al., 2010), which coordinates the simultaneous expression of both mitochondrial and nuclear genomes, and controls the mtDNA copy number (Figure 5A and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and C and a citation to Ljubicic et al., 2010, which describes TFAm's role.

claim: Treatment with GSK3357679A increases mitophagy in both WT and G2019S dopaminergic neurons of the SNpc.
source: In DA neurons of the SNpc, we found that treatment with GSK3357679A increased mitophagy in both WT and G2019S KI mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and B, demonstrating increased mitophagy in DA neurons with GSK3357679A treatment.

claim: Treatment with GSK3357679A restores G2019S mitophagy to base-line WT levels in dopaminergic neurons.
source: Importantly, treatment with GSK3357679A restored G2019S mitophagy to base-line WT levels (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and B, demonstrating rescue of mitophagy defect in G2019S DA neurons.

claim: GSK3357679A has no effect on mitophagy in LRRK2 KO dopaminergic neurons.
source: No difference was observable in the KO groups in presence of GSK3357679A, showing mitophagy effects are through on-target LRRK2 inhibition.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and B, demonstrating no effect of GSK3357679A in LRRK2 KO DA neurons.

claim: GSK3357679A increases mitophagy in cortical microglia in both WT and G2019S groups.
source: GSK3357679A increased mitophagy in the cortical microglia in both WT and G2019S groups (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C and D, demonstrating increased mitophagy in microglia with GSK3357679A treatment.

claim: GSK3357679A restores G2019S mitophagy levels to a value similar to the WT control group in cortical microglia.
source: Consistently, GSK3357679A restored G2019S mitophagy levels to a value similar to that detected in the control group (WT-V).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C and D, demonstrating rescue of mitophagy defect in G2019S microglia.

claim: GSK3357679A treatment recovers the increase in number of cortical microglia observed in LRRK2 G2019S KI mice.
source: Intriguingly, GSK3357679A treatment recovered the increase in number of cortical microglia observed in LRRK2 G2019S KI mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that LRRK2 kinase activity is a key contributor to regulation of microglial numbers in this mouse line.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, demonstrating normalization of microglial cell numbers with GSK3357679A treatment.

claim: GSK3357679A increases mitophagy levels in both WT and G2019S lungs.
source: In the lungs, we found that GSK3357679A increased mitophagy levels in both WT and G2019S KI animals (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E and F, demonstrating increased mitophagy in lungs with GSK3357679A treatment.

claim: GSK3357679A has no effect on mitophagy levels in the lungs of LRRK2 KO mice.
source: GSK3357679A had no effect on mitophagy levels in the lungs of LRRK2 KO mice (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E and F, demonstrating no effect of GSK3357679A in LRRK2 KO lungs.

claim: In the G2019S group, GSK3357679A elevates lung mitophagy levels to a value similar to the WT Vehicle group.
source: Importantly, in the G2019S group, GSK3357679A elevated mitophagy levels to a value similar to the WT Vehicle group, suggesting LRRK2-inhibition can also rescue the G2019S-mediated defect in mitophagy in lung.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E and F, demonstrating rescue of mitophagy defect in G2019S lungs.

claim: Enlarged lamellar bodies in Type-II pneumocytes are observed in the lungs of mice treated with GSK3357679A.
source: As observed for other LRRK2 inhibitors we observed enlarged lamellar bodies in Type-II pneumocytes in the lungs of mice treated with GSK3357679A, similar to that observed in LRRK2 KO mice (Figure 4A) and to what has been previously reported in the presence of other LRRK2 kinase inhibitors (Fell et al., 2015; Baptista et al., 2018; Fuji et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations and citations to Fell et al., 2015; Baptista et al., 2018; Fuji et al., 2015, which previously reported this phenotype.

claim: GSK3357679A has minimal effect on mitophagy in the kidney despite robust LRRK2 inhibition.
source: Consistent with KO mice, in the kidney we found that GSK3357679A had a minimal effect on mitophagy despite this organ exhibiting robust LRRK2 inhibition (compare Figure 4C and D with Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C, demonstrating minimal effect on kidney mitophagy.

claim: LRRK2 kinase activity inversely correlates with basal mitophagy levels, both in vitro and in vivo in specific cells and tissues.
source: Our work reveals that LRRK2 kinase activity inversely correlates with basal mitophagy levels, both in vitro and in vivo in specific cells and tissues.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined genetic and pharmacological data showing that increased LRRK2 activity reduces mitophagy and decreased activity increases mitophagy.

claim: The mitophagy defects are specific to certain cell types.
source: Strikingly, the mitophagy defects seemed to be specific to certain cell types. Indeed, we observed different effects in two different neuronal subpopulations and in two microglial subpopulations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that mitophagy changes were seen in DA neurons and cortical microglia but not in Purkinje neurons or astrocytes.

claim: Brain resident microglia have much higher LRRK2 levels and activity than neuronal populations.
source: Also of potential relevance, we observed a higher difference in mitophagy levels between genotypes in the cortical microglia than in the DA neurons. Brain resident microglia have been shown to have much higher LRRK2 levels and activity than neuronal populations, which could have implications for disease aetiology (Schapansky et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Schapansky et al., 2015, which reports higher LRRK2 levels in microglia.

claim: This study provides the first in vivo evidence that pathogenic LRRK2 directly impairs basal mitophagy.
source: The work presented here shows for the first time that pathogenic LRRK2 mutations can alter basal mitophagy in clinically relevant cell populations in vivo.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings, based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Loss of PINK1 does not impact mitophagy induced upon LRRK2 inhibition.
source: However, we found that loss of PINK1 (and hence a block in Parkin activation) did not impact mitophagy induced upon LRRK2 inhibition and nor did it alter the magnitude of Parkin-dependent mitophagy that occurs following mitochondrial depolarisation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G and H, demonstrating similar mitophagy induction in WT and PINK1 KO cells with GSK3357679A.

claim: Loss of PINK1 or Parkin activity does not significantly alter basal mitophagy rates in vivo.
source: This fits well with previous data generated by us and others, which demonstrates that loss of PINK1 or Parkin activity does not significantly alter basal mitophagy rates in vivo (McWilliams et al., 2018a; McWilliams et al., 2018b; Lee et al., 2018; Wrighton et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to McWilliams et al., 2018a; McWilliams et al., 2018b; Lee et al., 2018; Wrighton et al., 2021, which demonstrate that PINK1/Parkin are not required for basal mitophagy.

claim: The PINK1/Parkin pathway drives mitophagy under distinct types of extreme mitochondrial stress, such as that caused during repeated exhaustive exercise.
source: We take this to mean that the PINK1/Parkin pathway drives mitophagy under distinct types of extreme mitochondrial stress, such as that caused during repeated exhaustive exercise (Sliter et al., 2018), in contrast to the basally regulated LRRK2 pathway described here.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sliter et al., 2018, which demonstrates PINK1/Parkin-dependent mitophagy during exercise stress.

claim: If loss of stress-induced PINK1/Parkin-dependent mitophagy can lead to PD, then loss of LRRK2-regulated basal mitophagy could also contribute.
source: Regardless, if loss of stress-induced PINK1/Parkin-dependent mitophagy can lead to PD, then it is reasonable to assume that loss of LRRK2-regulated basal mitophagy could also contribute.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the parallel between PINK1/Parkin and LRRK2 pathways in PD.

claim: Impaired mitophagy may be a common theme in PD pathology.
source: These data now imply that impaired mitophagy may be a common theme in PD pathology.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that multiple PD-associated genes (PINK1, Parkin, LRRK2) affect mitophagy.

claim: Patient derived fibroblasts bearing G2019S or R1441C LRRK2 variants show results consistent with the in vitro cell assays and observations in vivo presented in this study.
source: In vitro assays in patient derived fibroblasts bearing G2019S or R1441C LRRK2 variants are consistent with our in vitro cell assays and observations in vivo (Wauters et al., 2020; Bonello et al., 2019; Korecka et al., 2019; Hsieh et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wauters et al., 2020; Bonello et al., 2019; Korecka et al., 2019; Hsieh et al., 2016, which report similar findings in patient cells.

claim: LRRK2 has been shown to phosphorylate a subset of Rab GTPases.
source: LRRK2 has been shown to phosphorylate a subset of Rab GTPases (Steger et al., 2016) and, given the roles of Rabs in membrane trafficking, it is tempting to suggest that they may be key in regulating this mitophagy pathway (Pfeffer, 2018; Pfeffer, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Steger et al., 2016; Pfeffer, 2018; Pfeffer, 2017, which describe LRRK2's phosphorylation of Rabs and their role in trafficking.

claim: Lysosomal overload stress induces translocation of Rab7L1 and LRRK2 to lysosomes, leading to LRRK2 activation and stabilisation of Rab8 and Rab10 through phosphorylation.
source: It has been recently shown that lysosomal overload stress induces translocation of Rab7L1 and LRRK2 to lysosomes (Eguchi et al., 2018). This leads to the activation of LRRK2 and the stabilisation of Rab8 and Rab10 through phosphorylation.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Eguchi et al., 2018, which describes LRRK2 translocation and activation at lysosomes.

claim: LRRK2 mutations inhibit the mitochondrial localisation of Rab10.
source: Another recent study showed that LRRK2 mutations inhibit the mitochondrial localisation of Rab10 (Wauters et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wauters et al., 2020, which reports altered Rab10 localization with LRRK2 mutations.

claim: LRRK2 activity can influence phagosome trafficking to lysosomes.
source: Previous work has shown that LRRK2 activity can influence phagosome trafficking to lysosomes (Härtlova et al., 2018) and recently it was shown that LRRK2 can influence axonal autophagosome trafficking via the motor adaptor protein JIP4 (Boecker et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Härtlova et al., 2018; Boecker et al., 2021, which describe LRRK2's role in trafficking.

claim: LRRK2 regulation of JIP4 has been implicated in lysosome tubulation.
source: Relatedly and also of relevance, LRRK2 regulation of JIP4 has been implicated in lysosome tubulation (Bonet-Ponce et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bonet-Ponce et al., 2020, which describes LRRK2's role in lysosome tubulation via JIP4.

claim: Deleterious mitochondrial phenotypes have been observed in LRRK2 G2019S patient-derived cells.
source: Indeed, deleterious mitochondrial phenotypes have been observed in LRRK2 G2019S patient-derived cells (Delcambre et al., 2020; Mortiboys et al., 2010; Sanders et al., 2014), although further work is needed to clarify if this is a cause or consequence of impaired mitophagy.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Delcambre et al., 2020; Mortiboys et al., 2010; Sanders et al., 2014, which report mitochondrial defects in patient cells.

claim: GSK3357679A led to activation of mitochondrial biogenesis via PGC-1β and not PGC-1α.
source: It is important to note that GSK3357679A led to activation of mitochondrial biogenesis via PGC-1β and not PGC-1α.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and C, demonstrating increased PGC-1β but not PGC-1α with GSK3357679A treatment.

claim: A careful balance between mitochondrial turnover and biogenesis has been shown to occur previously.
source: While further work will be needed to validate this, a careful balance between mitochondrial turnover and biogenesis has been shown to occur previously (Palikaras et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Palikaras et al., 2015, which describes the balance between mitophagy and biogenesis.

claim: Extensive preclinical studies in vivo failed to detect any effects of LRRK2 inhibition on lung function.
source: However, it is important to note that extensive preclinical studies in vivo failed to detect any effects of LRRK2 inhibition on lung function (Baptista et al., 2020) and likewise, no deleterious effects have been reported for LRRK2 kinase inhibitors in clinical studies for Parkinson's disease thus far (Biogen Denali Therapeutics Inc, 2021a; Biogen Denali Therapeutics Inc, 2021b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Baptista et al., 2020; Biogen Denali Therapeutics Inc, 2021a; Biogen Denali Therapeutics Inc, 2021b, which report safety data for LRRK2 inhibitors.

claim: No deleterious effects have been reported for LRRK2 kinase inhibitors in clinical studies for Parkinson's disease thus far.
source: However, it is important to note that extensive preclinical studies in vivo failed to detect any effects of LRRK2 inhibition on lung function (Baptista et al., 2020) and likewise, no deleterious effects have been reported for LRRK2 kinase inhibitors in clinical studies for Parkinson's disease thus far (Biogen Denali Therapeutics Inc, 2021a; Biogen Denali Therapeutics Inc, 2021b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Biogen Denali Therapeutics Inc, 2021a; Biogen Denali Therapeutics Inc, 2021b, which report clinical trial safety data.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of LRRK2 is a rational mitophagy-rescue approach and potential PD therapy.
source: This study provides the first in vivo evidence that pathogenic LRRK2 directly impairs basal mitophagy, a process with strong links to idiopathic Parkinson's disease, and demonstrates that pharmacological inhibition of LRRK2 is a rational mitophagy-rescue approach and potential PD therapy.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined data showing that LRRK2 inhibition can rescue mitophagy defects in G2019S mice.

claim: The mito-QC reporter is localized to mitochondria by an outer mitochondrial targeting sequence derived from residues 101–152 of the protein FIS1.
source: In the mito-QC model, which monitors mitophagy, the tandem tag is localised to mitochondria (by an outer mitochondrial targeting sequence derived from residues 101–152 of the protein FIS1).
evidence: This describes the technical design of the mito-QC reporter system.

claim: The auto-QC reporter is localized to autophagosomes by conjugation to the N-terminus of MAP1LC3b.
source: In the auto-QC model, which monitors general (macro)autophagy, the tandem tag is localised to autophagosomes (by conjugation to the N-terminus of MAP1LC3b).
evidence: This describes the technical design of the auto-QC reporter system.

claim: When a mitochondrion or autophagosome is delivered to lysosomes, the low lysosomal luminal pH quenches the GFP signal but not mCherry.
source: For both models, when a mitochondrion or autophagosome is delivered to lysosomes, the low lysosomal luminal pH is sufficient to quench the GFP signal, but not that from mCherry.
evidence: This describes the principle behind the tandem fluorescent reporter system.

claim: The degree of mitophagy or general autophagy can be determined by the appearance of mCherry-only puncta, which represent mito/autolysosomes.
source: Hence, the degree of mitophagy or general autophagy can be determined by the appearance of mCherry-only puncta, which represent mito/autolysosomes (Figure 1A and D).
evidence: This describes how the reporter systems quantify mitophagy and autophagy.

claim: Mitophagy is a form of autophagy.
source: Given that mitophagy is a form of autophagy, the use of both models allows us to monitor the specificity of autophagy in vivo.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the relationship between mitophagy and autophagy.

claim: A large disruption of autophagy in general will also influence mitophagy.
source: A large disruption of autophagy in general will also influence mitophagy, whereas a block in mitophagy, which likely represents a small fraction of the total autophagy occurring at any one time, will tend to have little influence on the total autophagic levels.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the relationship between general autophagy and mitophagy.

claim: A block in mitophagy will tend to have little influence on the total autophagic levels.
source: A large disruption of autophagy in general will also influence mitophagy, whereas a block in mitophagy, which likely represents a small fraction of the total autophagy occurring at any one time, will tend to have little influence on the total autophagic levels.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the relationship between mitophagy and total autophagy.
